summary: This Wikipedia-derived note describes the Rhine river and its delta. It covers the course from Lake Constance through Switzerland, the German-Swiss and Franco-German borders, and the split into Waal, Nederrijn and other arms in the Netherlands, along with the origin of the river's name. It also covers Roman-era legions along the Rhine, its political history through the Holy Roman Empire and France, the formation and modern management of the delta, and its role in World War II and Cold War planning.
one_line: Overview of the Rhine river, its course from the Swiss Alps to the North Sea, its delta, name origins, and history.
key_facts: The Rhine-Meuse Delta is the most important natural region of the Netherlands and begins near Millingen aan de Rijn at the division of the Rhine into Waal and Nederrijn.
The Rhine is the longest river in Germany.
The Moselle contributes an average discharge of more than 300 m3/s (11,000 cu ft/s) to the Rhine.
As it approaches the Dutch border, the Rhine has an annual mean discharge of 2,290 m3/s (81,000 cu ft/s) and an average width of 400 m (1,300 ft).
The Aare more than doubles the Rhine's water discharge, to an average of nearly 1,000 m3/s, and provides more than a fifth of the discharge at the Dutch border.
The Aare contains waters from the 4,274 m (14,022 ft) summit of Finsteraarhorn, the highest point of the Rhine basin.
The Rhine is the second-longest river in Central and Western Europe after the Danube, at about 1,230 km (760 mi), with an average discharge of about 2,900 m3/s (100,000 cu ft/s).
The Rhine begins in the Swiss canton of Graubünden in the southeastern Swiss Alps and empties into the North Sea in the Netherlands.
The biggest city on the Rhine is Cologne, Germany, with a population of more than 1,050,000 people.
The Rhine flows as the Hochrhein from Lake Constance, passes the Rhine Falls, and turns north at the Rhine knee at Basel, leaving Switzerland.
The name Rhine derives from the Gaulish name Rēnos, adapted in Roman-era geography (1st century BC) as Greek Rhēnos and Latin Rhenus.
Two thirds of the Rhine's water flows west through the Waal and then merges with the Meuse before entering the North Sea through the Hollands Diep and Haringvliet estuaries.
The Romans kept eight legions in five bases along the Rhine, with the actual number depending on whether a state or threat of war existed.
The Rhine bridge at Arnhem was a central focus of the battle for Arnhem during the failed Operation Market Garden of September 1944.
The Ludendorff Bridge at Remagen was captured intact by U.S. forces after the Germans failed to demolish it.
